title: More Typos, Fewer Em Dashes: Writers Are Creating an Anti-AI ‘Literary Counterculture’
excerpt: Novelists, journalists, and power LinkedIn posters are embracing first-person narratives and idiosyncrasies to avoid being mistaken for chat bots.
content_html:
Last year, when the novelist Laura Brooke Robson began writing Love Is an Algorithm—a love story between the cofounder of an AI dating app and a musician trying to survive in the age of large language models—she took extra care not to sound like AI herself.

She wrote sentences she doubts she would have attempted before the advent of LLMs, avoiding what she calls “wishy-washy metaphors,” and took “a more winding path to avoid an em dash or a tripartite list.”

Since the widespread adoption of LLMs, Robson says her writing has fundamentally changed for the better, becoming a deliberate inverse of what she sees as AI’s default lack of style.

“I find myself writing less mechanically,” she says. “I have this urge to make little mistakes, like winks to the reader, to show that there’s a human behind the words. Like: What if I just invented a phrase? What if I did something unexpected with my punctuation?”

Robson is part of a larger cohort of writers who are practicing what could be called an anti-AI writing style. Across journalism, criticism, creative writing, and especially among compulsive LinkedIn posters, writers are converging on a set of choices that implicitly resist the trappings of AI-generated prose.

The style mostly takes shape through negation, often of the obvious AI tells, like lists of three, passive voice, not x but y, and em dashes. But it also prizes idiosyncrasy as its overriding principle, tapping into specific first-person anecdotes and eccentric similes that demonstrate the necessary drudgery of writing.

“I think AI could absolutely trigger a literary counterculture,” says Robson. “It seems to me that literary fiction will shift even further in the direction of the weird, the esoteric, while personalization takes hold of commercial fiction.”

Throughout the publishing world, allegations of AI have been troubling authors. In March, Hachette pulled Mia Ballard’s horror novel Shy Girl after speculation spread online that its writer had heavily utilized AI, a claim she rejected. Ballard, who says she has new writing forthcoming, has had to restrategize. “Having my writing feel more real and authentic is my number one priority,” she says, in addition to editing her own writing because she claims an editor she hired ran the book through AI software. “That is what bit me in the ass the first time.” Hachette did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Likewise, Steven Rosenbaum’s book The Future of Truth, an examination of “how AI transforms reality,” was purported to include multiple fabricated quotations generated by AI, which Rosenbaum later admitted was true.

Ellena Savage, an Australian novelist and academic whose prose tends towards complex-compound sentences inspired by Victorian literature, says she has “sadly been victimized by thoughts of chatbots.” “AI has stolen several syntactical conventions I once held dear. I miss over-deploying the em dash. I miss the rule of three, which was so satisfying. Now what—the rule of two? Five? Seven? 10?”

Across magazines and digital publications, this anti-AI counterstyle is reshaping in-house style and editorial practice too. Richard Fisher, an honorary professor at University College London and editor at online culture magazine Aeon, says AI has prompted him to encourage writers “to be more human” and write more conversationally. “We don't want to sand out the rough edges, because AI cannot write prose as spiky or idiosyncratic as humans. Writers might not want to change their practice, but some might be forced into it.”

Mano Sundaresan became Pitchfork’s head of editorial content in July 2024, around the time LLMs became more mainstream. Coming from a blogging background, he encouraged writers “towards their own voice,” something he says, in hindsight, “could have also come from this AI turn.” He and his fellow editors have since sent writers a memo stating that no AI may be used when filing review copy, and encouraging first-person perspectives. (Pitchfork is owned by Condé Nast, which also owns WIRED.)

content_html_zh:
去年，当小说家劳拉·布鲁克·罗布森 (Laura Brooke Robson) 开始撰写《爱情是一种算法》（Love is an Algorithm）——一个人工智能约会应用程序的联合创始人和一位试图在大语言模型时代生存的音乐家之间的爱情故事时——她格外小心，不要让自己听起来像人工智能。

她怀疑自己在法学硕士出现之前是否会尝试写一些句子，避免使用她所说的“空洞的隐喻”，并采取了“一条更曲折的道路来避免长破折号或三方清单”。

罗布森说，自从法学硕士被广泛采用以来，她的写作已经从根本上发生了改善，成为她认为人工智能默认缺乏风格的故意反面。

“我发现自己写作不再机械化，”她说。 “我有一种犯小错误的冲动，比如向读者眨眼，以表明文字背后有一个人。 比如：如果我发明了一个短语怎么办？ 如果我对标点符号做了一些意想不到的事情怎么办？”

罗布森是众多作家中的一员，他们正在实践所谓的反人工智能写作风格。 在新闻、批评、创意写作中，尤其是在LinkedIn上强迫性发帖者中，作家们正在做出一系列选择，这些选择隐含地抵制人工智能生成的散文的陷阱。

这种风格主要是通过否定来形成的，通常是明显的人工智能告诉，如三列表、被动语态、不是 x 而是 y 和 em 破折号。 但它也将特质视为最重要的原则，利用具体的第一人称轶事和古怪的明喻来展示写作所必需的苦差事。

“我认为人工智能绝对会引发文学反文化，”罗布森说。 “在我看来，文学小说将进一步朝着怪异、深奥的方向转变，而商业小说则将走向个性化。”

在整个出版界，对人工智能的指控一直困扰着作者。 今年 3 月，阿歇特公司下架了米娅·巴拉德 (Mia Ballard) 的恐怖小说《害羞女孩》(Shy Girl)，因为网上流传着该小说的作者大量使用人工智能的猜测，但她否认了这一说法。 巴拉德说她即将有新的写作，她不得不重新制定策略。 “让我的作品感觉更加真实和真实是我的首要任务，”她说，除了编辑自己的作品之外，因为她声称她聘请的一名编辑通过人工智能软件来编辑这本书。 “这就是第一次咬我屁股的原因。” 阿歇特没有立即回应置评请求。

同样，史蒂文·罗森鲍姆（Steven Rosenbaum）的书《真理的未来》（The Future of Truth）探讨了“人工智能如何改变现实”，据称其中包含了人工智能生成的多个捏造的引文，罗森鲍姆后来承认这些引文是真实的。

澳大利亚小说家和学者埃琳娜·萨维奇 (Ellena Savage) 的散文倾向于受维多利亚时代文学启发的复杂复合句，她说她“不幸地成为了聊天机器人思想的受害者”。 “人工智能窃取了我曾经珍视的几个语法约定。 我怀念过度部署破折号的感觉。 我怀念三人法则，那是非常令人满意的。 现在怎么样——二人法则？ 五？ 七？ 10?”

在杂志和数字出版物中，这种反人工智能的反风格也在重塑内部风格和编辑实践。 伦敦大学学院名誉教授、在线文化杂志 Aeon 编辑理查德·费舍尔 (Richard Fisher) 表示，人工智能促使他鼓励作家“变得更加人性化”，并更多地以对话方式写作。 “我们不想打磨粗糙的边缘，因为人工智能无法像人类一样写出尖锐或独特的散文。 作家可能不想改变他们的做法，但有些人可能被迫这样做。”

Mano Sundaresan 于 2024 年 7 月成为 Pitchfork 的编辑内容主管，当时法学硕士变得更加主流。 来自博客背景的他鼓励作家“发出自己的声音”，事后他说，“这也可能来自人工智能的转变。” 此后，他和他的编辑同事们向作家发送了一份备忘录，声明在提交评论副本时不得使用人工智能，并鼓励第一人称视角。 （Pitchfork 归康泰纳仕集团所有，该公司还拥有《连线》杂志。）
